claims.text: Machines generating IDs should not have to coordinate with each other, for high availability within and across data centres.
IDs had to stay under 64 bits and be sortable without loading the full objects they represent. The guarantee on ordering is that IDs are k-sorted, that is, roughly time ordered.
The performance target was a minimum of 10k IDs per second per process.

41 bits of time at millisecond precision, which with a custom epoch lasts 69 years; 10 bits of configured machine ID, allowing up to 1024 machines; and 12 bits of sequence number, which rolls over every 4096 per machine.
The generator has protection to avoid the sequence rolling over within the same millisecond.
The system clock should be kept accurate with NTP, and Snowflake protects against non-monotonic clocks, that is, clocks that run backwards.

recall.prompt: How are the bits of a Snowflake ID divided?

answer.text: 41 bits of millisecond time, 10 bits of machine ID, 12 bits of sequence number.

recall.prompt: How many machines and how many IDs per millisecond per machine does that layout allow?

answer.text: Up to 1024 machines, and a sequence that rolls over every 4096 per machine.

recall.prompt: What clock hazard does Snowflake guard against?

answer.text: Non-monotonic clocks, meaning clocks that run backwards.
